key_facts: **IgA vasculitis** (Henoch–Schönlein purpura) is the commonest childhood vasculitis: **palpable purpura** on the buttocks and legs.
Tetrad: purpura, arthralgia/arthritis, abdominal pain (intussusception risk) and **renal involvement** (haematuria, proteinuria).
Often follows an upper respiratory infection; ages 3–10.
First exclude **meningococcal sepsis** in an unwell child with a non-blanching rash.
Supportive care; monitor **urine and BP** for 6–12 months; adults have more renal disease.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: The **commonest childhood vasculitis** (~20 per 100,000 children/year). A systemic **IgA-immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis** affecting skin, joints, gut and kidneys. **~90% of cases are in children** (peak 3–10 years; ~75% under 8; slightly more boys), but it **does occur in adults**, where renal disease is more often severe.

sub: About 20 per 100,000 children per year; autumn and winter; adults less often but more severely.

ul: **"The rash settled, so follow-up can stop"**: nephritis can appear weeks to months later.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Abnormal **IgA1** forms immune complexes that lodge in small vessels.

mech.t: Galactose-deficient IgA1 is produced after a mucosal infection.
IgA complexes deposit in small vessel walls in skin, gut, joints and kidney.
Neutrophils damage vessels and red cells leak: palpable purpura.
mech.caption: Small-vessel vasculitis: immune complexes on the vessel wall attract neutrophils that fragment and damage it, letting red cells leak out (palpable purpura).

mech.t: Mesangial IgA deposits cause haematuria and proteinuria.

blocks: **Galactose-deficient IgA1** forms immune complexes (with anti-glycan IgG) that deposit in vessel walls and the glomerular mesangium. It often follows an **upper respiratory infection** — **group A β-haemolytic streptococcus** is the most reported trigger (positive throat swabs in 10–30%, raised ASO in 20–50%). Other triggers: parainfluenza, adenovirus, *Mycoplasma*, parvovirus, drugs, vaccines, malignancy in adults.

histo: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA on direct IF of a new lesion.

ul: **Palpable purpura** (100%, required): symmetrical on the **buttocks, legs, ankles and extensor arms**, ± urticarial and bullous/necrotic lesions; scrotal oedema; oedema of the scalp/face in toddlers.
**Arthralgia/arthritis** (~75%): knees and ankles, transient and non-erosive.
**Abdominal pain** (~65%) ± GI bleeding (~30%), **intussusception** (ileo-ileal — 1–5%), pancreatitis.

**Renal** (~30–50%): microscopic/macroscopic **haematuria**, proteinuria, nephritic/nephrotic syndrome, hypertension, raised creatinine. Usually within **4–6 weeks** (up to 6 months). The main long-term risk: ~1–2% of children progress to CKD; higher if nephrotic/nephritic at onset.
Rare: orchitis/testicular torsion mimic, CNS involvement, pulmonary haemorrhage.

**EULAR/PRINTO/PRES classification (children):** **purpura or petechiae, lower-limb predominant (mandatory)** + ≥1 of: abdominal pain; histology with IgA deposition; arthritis/arthralgia; renal involvement (proteinuria >0.3 g/24 h or uACR >30 mg/mmol, or haematuria/red-cell casts).
**Bloods:** **FBC + film (platelets normal — excludes ITP/leukaemia)**, clotting, U&E/creatinine, albumin, CRP; ASO ± throat swab; IgA (raised in ~50%; not diagnostic).
**Urinalysis + BP** at diagnosis; **urine ACR/PCR** if proteinuria.
**Biopsy** only if atypical (adults, uncertain diagnosis): LCV with **perivascular IgA and C3 on DIF**. Renal biopsy if significant proteinuria or impaired function.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: **Meningococcal septicaemia** (unwell, fever, rapidly spreading non-blanching rash — must be excluded first), **ITP** (low platelets, flat petechiae/bruising, well), **acute leukaemia** (pallor, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, abnormal FBC), **acute haemorrhagic oedema of infancy**, non-accidental injury, cryoglobulinaemia, GPA, SLE, post-streptococcal GN, HUS (diarrhoea, anaemia, low platelets, AKI), papular-purpuric gloves-and-socks syndrome (parvovirus), scurvy, drug vasculitis.

sections.title: Management

ul: **Exclude sepsis first.** A child with non-blanching rash who is unwell or febrile → **NICE NG240**: treat as **meningococcal disease** — 999. Give **IM/IV benzylpenicillin** in primary care if it does not delay transfer.

**Most children are managed at home:** rest, **paracetamol** for joint pain. **NSAIDs** may be used for arthralgia if there is **no renal involvement** and no GI bleeding (avoid in renal disease). Elevate the legs for purpura.
**Oral corticosteroids** may help **severe abdominal pain/arthritis/orchitis** (specialist advice). They do **not prevent nephritis** and are not given routinely.

**Renal monitoring** (core primary-care task — the course mentions it only briefly): **urinalysis and BP** at presentation and then regularly for **at least 6 months** — typically **weekly for the first month, then every 2 weeks to month 3, monthly to month 6, then at 12 months** (CKS/UK paediatric nephrology practice — check the current CKS schedule). Any proteinuria or hypertension → paediatric/renal referral.
**Recurrence** occurs in ~1/3, usually within 4 months.
**Pregnancy:** women with a history of HSP nephritis need BP/urine monitoring in pregnancy (pre-eclampsia risk).

blocks: Within IP scope for a well child or adult with typical HSP and normal urine/BP: analgesia, safety-netting, arranging the urinalysis/BP schedule and recognising when to escalate. Paediatric IPs: follow local competence frameworks for children.

refer.t: Child unwell, febrile or with spreading non-blanching rash: treat as **meningococcal disease** until proven otherwise.
Severe abdominal pain or blood in stool: possible **intussusception**, same-day paediatric review.
Proteinuria, haematuria or high BP: paediatric nephrology advice; keep checking urine for 6–12 months.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Child unwell, febrile or with spreading non-blanching rash: treat as **meningococcal disease** until proven otherwise.
Severe abdominal pain or blood in stool: possible **intussusception**, same-day paediatric review.
Proteinuria, haematuria or high BP: paediatric nephrology advice; keep checking urine for 6–12 months.

blocks: Unwell/febrile child or **atypical rash** (exclude meningococcal sepsis/leukaemia); **severe abdominal pain**, bloody stools, signs of **intussusception**; **testicular pain/swelling** (exclude torsion); **renal involvement** — macroscopic haematuria, proteinuria ≥2+ or uPCR >100 mg/mmol (nephrotic range — CKS), oedema, **hypertension**, raised creatinine; adults (higher renal risk — refer for assessment); diagnostic uncertainty; low platelets.

ul: Nephritis and chronic kidney disease, intussusception, orchitis.
Most children recover in 4–6 weeks; recurrence in a third.

pearls: "**HSP = purpura with a NORMAL platelet count.**" If platelets are low, it is not HSP.
Give the family a **urine dipstick plan** and a written list of red flags (abdominal pain, blood in urine/stools, swollen testicles, headache, reduced urine output).
The rash can recur with activity/standing — reassure.

quiz.q: When should you think of IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura)?
quiz.a: A child (often 3–10 years) with palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks after a cold or sore throat, with sore joints or tummy pain.
IgA-containing immune complexes in small vessels of the skin, gut, joints and kidneys.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Exclude sepsis; BP and urine dipstick; FBC and clotting if unsure; simple analgesia; urine and BP monitoring for 6–12 months.
Meningococcal sepsis, leukaemia or ITP (check platelets), intussusception, nephritis.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Child unwell, febrile or with spreading non-blanching rash: treat as **meningococcal disease** until proven otherwise.
